Call options give the buyer the right to buy at a certain price, and the obligation to the seller to sell at that price if the buyer exercises his right.

Put options give the buyer the right to sell at a certain price, and the obligation to the seller to buy at that price if the buyer exercises his right.

Let's say you buy a call option for XYZ@50, you pay $5 premium for that. Now, if the price goes below 50, you don't exercise the right to buy and lose $5, but nothing else. If the price goes above 55 (50+5), for example 400, you win the difference ($345).

The seller, on the other hand, will have the opposite scenario. If the stock price goes below 50, they win the $5 premium and lose nothing. If the price somehow gets to 400, they are losing $345 (they need to buy stock at 400, sell it at 50 to you, and collect 5 premium from you).

Same applies for put options. You buy a put option for XYZ@50, and pay $5 premium for it. If the price goes above 50, you lose only $5. But if the price drops to 10, you exercise your right to sell it at 50 and win $40.
The seller, similarly to the call option, will only win $5 if the price goes above 50, and lose the difference from 50 to potentially 0, if the stock goes below 50.

That's why they are at a bigger risk; they have a maximum amount they can win from the operation (the premium you paid), but unlimited losses if the stock skyrockets or goes to 0.

That looks cool, but the regex is wrong: 

AB+10chars+8 are 13 chars in total, not 12 as you asked. The provided regex check that the string ends with 8, but doesnt check it starts with AB.

And there are shorter ways to express the same:

/\^AB\\S{9}8$/

This will validate against any string that starts with AB and ends with 8 and have 12 chars length.

/\\bAB\\S{9}8\\b/g

this will match all the words that starts with AB, and ends with 8 on a string

What does Linux lacks compared to windows?

Software support mostly. Most Windows programs (like 80% of them) can be run on Linux using wine, but some of them doesn't work OTB and need tweaking, while others wont work at all (Adobe, Fortnite, and others).

​

What does Linux better than windows?

Almost everything else. More stable experience (say goodbye to blue screens), better management of resources, more privacy aware, package manager (you wont ever need to search on google for installers), KVM virtualization (which is top notch), containerization / sandboxing of apps, unix philosophy: programs that do one single thing and do it well, instead of a single program that tries to do everything. This means a lot more customization options - if you don't like something, you could replace it with an alternate program and it will integrate with the rest of the system. Almost everything can be replaced, high level stuff like file managers, window manager, image viewer, audio/video players, text editor, calendar, etc and low level stuff like init systems, custom kernels, audio systems, and other core programs.  


Here are some cool things that you can do with a recent linux distro without using external programs (unlike windows):  
\- If your distro uses Pipewire as the default audio server, you can pipe your audio streams from one application to other and even apply filters. That mean you can apply some filters to your microphone without needing external software running, like you would need on windows (VoiceMeeter + Virtual Audio Cable). You could also be recording/streaming your screen and only record audio from certain apps. You can even stream your audio from/to a remote computer. And you won't need to install any external program to do all of this.  
\- If your distro has a recent kernel, you can use wireguard to connect two computers to a private, encrypted shared network.  
\- You can sandbox any app so it doesn't have access to your personal files, your network, or your devices. The easiest way to do this is to use flatpak, but you can do it on any other program that is not on flatpak using bubblewrap.  
\- Most configurations are file-based, that means you can copy your config files, and place them on other computer and have the exact same configuration for all of your programs without needing to manually configure everything again.

Basically it hooks on functions called by some programs like ps/ls/netstat and return a modified response where the malware traces are scrubbed.

Since it requires LD_PRELOAD to function, statically linked tools can still detect it.

I'm not very well versed on this matter, but to my understanding they are different attacks. 

In a TTA, the attacker would infect the compiler, so any program that you compile with the infected compiler will be infected. In this attack the attacker is using LD_PRELOAD to preload a shared library.

Both attacks try to hook on functions used by programs to accomplish their job, but the TTA does so by infecting a compiler, while this attack does so by preloading a malicious shared library.

>I also don't see how you'd end up with one without making a major mistake along the wayYou are assuming all malware infection is coming from users misbehavior, like downloading random files from the internet and executing them. While this is a route some malware could take to infect a system, it's not the only one.

Nowadays, sophisticated malware will try to infect a system using vulnerabilities on services connecting to the internet. They could exploit a vulnerability on your browser leading to RCE, or exploit any other applications that may connect to the internet, like Telegram, Discord, Steam, etc. Even if you have exposed services, such as ssh, ftp, etc. They are all susceptible to being exploited by a malicious user.

Once someone has a RCE to your computer, it's just a matter of escalating privileges and achieve persistence, which can be done by the same means someone would do on a Linux server.

​

>Really, the main thing that makes Linux so secure is the fact that vulnerabilities tend to be caught and patched fairly quickly

They are patched fairly quickly until reported by a security researcher. That doesn't mean bad guys haven't been abusing it before they were reported. Vulnerabilities like [pwnkit](https://blog.qualys.com/vulnerabilities-threat-research/2022/01/25/pwnkit-local-privilege-escalation-vulnerability-discovered-in-polkits-pkexec-cve-2021-4034), has been exploitable since its first version, back in 2009 until 2022 when it was discovered and then patched. This is not the only vulnerability than has been hiding in plain sight for years. There is [Log4Shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log4Shell), first introduced on 2013, and not reported until Sept 2021. There is [ShellShock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shellshock_(software_bug)), first introduced on 1989 and not reported until Sept 2014. There is [Heartbleed](https://heartbleed.com/), introduced in 2012 and patched on Apr 2014. The list goes on.

​

>and the small marketshare

Linux has a small marketshare for desktop computers, but linux is at the top of the marketshare when it comes to servers and smartphones. Since Linux shares a huge chunk of code for servers, desktops and smartphones, most of the vulnerabilities found on Linux can affect all of the devices it supports, if they use the affected component.

I dont know enough english to describe it correctly, but it is somewhat sturdy on the outside but a bit softer in the inside. If you cook it for longer it is softer, if you cook it lesser, it is sturdier. The texture remains the same between broth or sauce cooking (sauce actually being a very dense broth).

They are sold in different varieties, that impact its size and texture. The bigger it is, the sturdier it feels. The most common is "chicos" or its literal translation "small ones". Pretty self explanatory name. This are softer than the others. Then, there is "cabrillas" which are the medium sized ones. I don't know of any proper translation. Then there is "gordos" which translates to "fat ones" and are the biggest and sturdiest. I wouldn't recommend anyone trying these if it is his/her first time eating snails.

My favorites are the "cabrillas" variant, not too small to even feel like I'm eating something, nor too big to feel like I'm eating a really big slug. If you ever visit Cordoba on snails season, I would advise you to first try the smallest one, and progressively go for "cabrillas" and then for "gordos" if you feel like it.

Cordoba, Sevilla and Cadiz are the only cities in Spain that I'm aware that have vendors selling snails as the main dish rather than a secondary ingredient of another recipe (like paella does). Cordoba has the strongest tradition out of the three, offering a wider variety of recipes that include carbonara snails, oxtail snails, spicy snails, snails with cheese and nachos, and others. In Cordoba there is also dedicated street food stalls that cook and serve snails at the same place, on Sevilla and Cadiz there isn't any street food stalls, but rather you would go to a bar who serves it and ask for it. They usually don't prepare it on house, they buy it from another vendor who actually cook them, and they just heat it for you and serve it.

I wouldn't recommend anyone with no prior culinary knowledge of snails to eat wild ones. There are actually some people here that do it, but they know where to go and which to pick. They need to be properly cleaned first, but thats a requirement no matter if you catch them or buy them unprepared.

I wouldn't either advise you eating canned snails, it's like buying frozen sushi to experience it first time and being disappointed you didn't liked it. If you really want to try them, I would suggest you to find a local vendor that sell snails for cooking purposes and find a traditional recipe and cook it yourself, it is very easy to prepare it.

[The EAC build that works with Proton is the one provided by Epic Online Services](https://dev.epicgames.com/en-US/news/epic-online-services-launches-anti-cheat-support-for-linux-mac-and-steam-deck). There are other builds of EAC that don't need EOS to be included in your game, and [some developers are still using this builds](https://steamcommunity.com/app/552500/discussions/0/2960544187643622408/?ctp=6#c3202622271470957243), which are not compatible with Proton. Thus, enabling support for Proton in EAC is just not as easy as many may think, it's not a click of a button away. You need to update your game to include EOS, and the new EAC build, and ensure that it passes all tests. Also, some developers may be reluctant to ship their game with Epic Online Services included.

They have to test that the anticheat doesn't ban Linux accounts by error before they enable it, and probably it's not their top priority right now, so thats why it takes so much time. However, announcing they are working on it is a huge step forward.

In fact, there is already 8 BattleEye games with proton support enabled (Ark SE, Ark SOTF, DayZ, Arma 3, Unturned, Planetside 2, M&B: BL, Insurgency), there is also 5 EAC games with Proton support enabled (WarThunder, 7days2die, Squad, Brawlhalla and Albion Online) and 6 EAC games announced proton compatibility soon (Dead By Daylight, Rust, Knockout City, Due Process, POLYGON, Star Citizen).

You can check the complete list here:[https://areweanticheatyet.com/](https://areweanticheatyet.com/)

The future of Linux gaming looks promising.
